title: From 30 October, employers answer for harassment by clients and delegates unless they took all reasonable steps
seo_title: Employers liable for third-party harassment from 30 October
dek: The sixth commencement regulations under the Employment Rights Act 2025 bring in a new third-party harassment duty on 30 October and tighten the existing sexual harassment duty to all reasonable steps. Most tribunal claims about acts from 1 October get six months. What it means for crews among clients and delegates.
summary: From 30 October, employers are liable for third-party harassment unless they took all reasonable steps. Most claims on acts from 1 October get six months.
body:
From 30 October, an employer can be liable when its staff are harassed by a client, a contractor or someone at a conference, unless it took all reasonable steps to prevent it. The [Commencement No. 6 regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/1065/made) under the Employment Rights Act 2025 (SI 2026/1065) were made on 1 October, and regulation 3 brings sections 20, 21, 22, 56, 59, 60, 64 and 65 of the Act into force on 30 October, the last four "so far as not already in force".

Three of those matter on a show floor, and only one of them is a new duty. [Section 21](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2025/36/section/21) adds it to the Equality Act 2010: an employer "must not permit a third party to harass" one of its employees. [Section 20](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2025/36/section/20) tightens a duty that already exists. Employers have had to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of their employees since 26 October 2024, under [section 40A](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/section/40A) of the Equality Act; section 20 inserts "all" before "reasonable steps". [Section 22](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2025/36/section/22) is a power: "Regulations may specify steps that are to be regarded as 'reasonable'".

One change is already live. The time limit for most Employment Tribunal claims went from three months to six on 1 October, according to the government's [timeline](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/implementing-the-plan-to-make-work-pay-and-employment-rights-act/plan-to-make-work-pay-and-employment-rights-act-timeline-update), for things that happen from that date on.

## Who counts as a third party

[Acas](https://www.acas.org.uk/employment-rights-act-2025/harassment-law-changes) does not hedge: "On 30 October 2026 the law will change so employers will be liable for harassment from third parties." The next line is the one to pin up in the production office: "This will be unless you have taken all reasonable steps to prevent it." GOV.UK describes the same duty as "an obligation on employers not to permit the harassment of their employees by third parties".

Neither asks you to make a conference harassment-free by force of will. The question is what you did, and what you can show you did, before the doors opened.

Section 21 sets two conditions for liability: the harassment happened "in the course of" the employee's employment, and the employer "failed to take all reasonable steps". It says harass, not sexually harass, so the duty is not limited to sexual harassment. A third party is anyone other than the employer or one of its employees.

Acas's list of third parties reads like a call sheet: clients, "self-employed consultants, contractors or tradespeople" and "people at conferences or events". A hall full of delegates and a client who has found the free bar is, in our view, about as third-party as a workplace gets.

Freelancers are the awkward bit, and the word that decides it is "employee". [Section 83](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/section/83) of the Equality Act 2010 counts employment under "a contract personally to do work" as employment, and says references to an employee are read with that. On our reading, a freelancer booked to do the graphics personally is, for these sections, an employee of the AV company that booked them: covered by its duty, and not a third party to it. A freelancer outside that definition is a third party to the company, and so is the venue's duty manager, who is employed by the venue. We have not tested that against case law. [Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/10/uk-employment-rights-act-2025-october-reforms-taking-effect), a law firm, defines a third party as "anyone other than an employer or one of its employees", which is fair as a paraphrase but leaves section 83 out.

Morgan Lewis says an employee "will only need to show that third-party harassment took place during the course of their employment". It also describes an earlier rule, which it says was repealed in 2013, that made an employer liable only after harassment by a third party "on at least two occasions". That history is the firm's; we have not checked it against the statute.

The firm also lists a compensation uplift of up to 25% under its 30 October heading. That one is not new. [Section 124A](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/section/124A) of the Equality Act has applied since 26 October 2024: where a tribunal finds a breach of section 40 that involved, to any extent, sexual harassment, it "must consider" whether the employer also breached its section 40A(1) duty to prevent sexual harassment, and if so it "may order" an uplift of up to 25% of the compensation. What 30 October changes is the duty the uplift is measured against, which section 20 raises to all reasonable steps.

## Six months on the clock

The longer limit covers most claims. Breach of employment contract claims in Scotland come later: GOV.UK puts their change at 9 November 2026, and we have not seen the instrument behind that date. The transitional rule is [regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2026/954/regulation/4) of SI 2026/954: the amendments that bring in the longer limits "do not apply in any case where the relevant date occurs before 1st October 2026". For claims outside the enactments listed in the regulations' Schedule, which we have not read, the relevant date is "the date of the act, conduct, or failure complained of". Morgan Lewis thinks the longer limit "may also create substantially more uncertainty" for employers.

Our reading, in production terms: a bad night at a November awards dinner could still turn into a claim the following spring, long after the set has gone back to the workshop.

## The union piece

Section 59 covers trade union access to workplaces. [business.gov.uk](https://www.business.gov.uk/campaign/employment-changes/employers/trade-union-reform/) describes the 30 October start as "subject to parliamentary approval", but that page was last updated on 25 September, before the regulations were made. It has two details worth knowing if you run a small crew company. It says the Central Arbitration Committee "can only impose an access agreement where an employer employs 21 or more workers", and that employers "must respond to requests within 15 working days of the request being sent". It is less tidy about what comes next, giving 25 working days to negotiate in one place and saying the negotiation period "will be reduced to 15 working days" in another. We have not checked any of these figures against the Act.

## What comes after

Further out, GOV.UK has the unfair dismissal qualifying period falling to six months for dismissals from 1 January 2027. April 2027 brings a ban on blacklists drafted using AI and on blacklisting by third parties, and December 2027 the regulation of umbrella companies, which anyone paid through an umbrella will want to watch. GOV.UK adds: "All future dates remain subject to parliamentary processes and may change."

The regulations on reasonable steps have no date on GOV.UK, and section 22 makes them subject to the affirmative procedure, so Parliament has to approve them. Morgan Lewis expects them in 2027 or 2028 after consultation, which is a forecast, not a timetable. GOV.UK says they will "complement, not replace" the broader requirement to take all reasonable steps, so waiting for a checklist from Whitehall is not a plan.

## Where that leaves events

This is the part of the Act that reaches furthest into event work. Few jobs put staff among clients, delegates, venue teams and other companies' crews quite as relentlessly as ours.

The official guidance we read, from Acas, GOV.UK and business.gov.uk, says nothing about freelancers, so section 83 is doing all the work. On our reading, what matters is how you were booked rather than whether you call yourself self-employed. Whichever side of that line you land, you are a third party to every other company's crew on site, which makes you part of somebody else's risk. Our guess is that companies booking freelancers start putting conduct terms and a reporting route into booking confirmations, if only to show they thought about it.

The client is always right about the running order. From 30 October, that is where it stops.

confirmed.text: SI 2026/1065, made on 1 October 2026 as the sixth commencement regulations under the Employment Rights Act 2025, brings sections 20, 21, 22, 56, 59, 60, 64 and 65 into force on 30 October 2026, sections 59, 60, 64 and 65 each so far as not already in force.
Section 20 of the Act, headed "Employers to take all reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment", inserts "all" before "reasonable steps" in section 40A(1) of the Equality Act 2010.

Section 40A of the Equality Act 2010, the duty on employers to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of their employees, was inserted on 26 October 2024 by the Worker Protection (Amendment of Equality Act 2010) Act 2023.

Section 21 inserts section 40(1A) to (1C) into the Equality Act 2010: an employer must not permit a third party to harass an employee, is liable where the harassment is in the course of employment and it failed to take all reasonable steps, and a third party is anyone other than the employer or one of its employees; the duty is not limited to sexual harassment.
Section 22 inserts section 40B into the Equality Act 2010, under which regulations may specify steps to be regarded as reasonable, and those regulations are subject to the affirmative procedure.
Section 83 of the Equality Act 2010 defines employment to include employment under a contract personally to do work, and says references to an employee are to be read with that definition.

Section 124A of the Equality Act 2010, in force since 26 October 2024, says that where a section 40 contravention involved sexual harassment the tribunal must consider whether the employer also breached section 40A(1), and may order an uplift of no more than 25% of the compensation.

Regulation 4 of SI 2026/954 says the longer tribunal time limits do not apply where the relevant date occurs before 1 October 2026, and sets that date as the date of the act, conduct or failure complained of, with tables in its Schedule for specified enactments.

The GOV.UK timeline, updated on 22 October 2026, says the tribunal time limit increased from 3 to 6 months on 1 October 2026 (9 November 2026 for breach of employment contract claims in Scotland) and lists for 30 October an obligation on employers not to permit the harassment of their employees by third parties.

GOV.UK gives no date for regulations on reasonable steps, says they will complement, not replace, the broader requirement, lists a 6-month unfair dismissal qualifying period from 1 January 2027, AI-drafted blacklists banned in April 2027 and umbrella company regulation in December 2027, and says all future dates may change.

Acas says employers will be liable from 30 October 2026 for harassment from third parties, such as clients, contractors and people at conferences or events, unless they have taken all reasonable steps, and suggests reviewing contracts, putting up-to-date terms on individual bookings, telling customers the consequences and training staff.

business.gov.uk, last updated on 25 September 2026, says the union access right starts on 30 October subject to parliamentary approval, that the CAC can only impose an access agreement where an employer employs 21 or more workers, and that employers must respond to requests within 15 working days.

speculation.text: Morgan Lewis expects regulations defining reasonable steps to come into force in 2027 or 2028 after consultation; GOV.UK gives no date for them.
Morgan Lewis says the longer tribunal time limit may create substantially more uncertainty for employers.

Morgan Lewis says an earlier rule, which it says was repealed in 2013, made employers liable for third-party harassment only after it happened on at least two occasions; we have not checked that against the statute.

Our reading of section 83 is that a freelancer booked on a contract to do the work personally is an employee of the booking company for these sections, so covered by its duty and not a third party to it; we have not tested that against case law.

impact:
**AV and production companies.** The third-party duty is yours from 30 October. On our reading of section 83 of the Equality Act, it covers freelancers you book on a contract to do the work personally as well as the staff on your payroll. Acas's suggested steps map onto event work with little translation:

- Review client, customer and supplier contracts and terms. On a job, that means the client contract, the venue agreement and the terms you send to freelancers and sub-hire companies.
- Make sure individual bookings carry up-to-date terms. Acas's example is hotel room bookings; for an event company, read that as each job confirmation, not a framework agreement signed years ago.
- Tell customers the consequences of harassing workers. A line in the client brief and in the delegate joining instructions costs nothing.
- Train crew in staff safety and de-escalation, before the busy weeks rather than after the incident.

Acas says taking all reasonable steps "means doing what is possible with the available resources". We read that as a bar that moves with the size of the company, not a licence to do nothing.

One clause of our own, not one Acas suggests: the right to withdraw a crew member from a situation where they are being harassed, without that counting as a failure to deliver.

**On the day.** Name someone on site, who is not the client, that crew can go to. Write incidents down the same night: what happened, when, who was told and what was done. If a step was considered and not taken, write down why.

**Freelance crew.** The guidance pages do not mention you, but the Act reaches you through section 83 of the Equality Act. Our reading: booked on a contract to do the work personally, you count as the booking company's employee for these sections, and its duty covers you. Outside that definition, you are a third party to that company. Either way, you are a third party to every other company's staff on site, so expect conduct terms to start turning up in bookings. If something happens to you on a job, write it down that night and tell whoever booked you.

**The tribunal clock.** For most claims about acts on or after 1 October, the window is six months. Keep incident notes, and the emails around them, for at least that long.

**Small companies and union requests.** business.gov.uk says the CAC can only impose an access agreement where an employer has 21 or more workers, and gives employers 15 working days to respond to an access request. It is not consistent about the negotiation period that follows, and we have not checked either figure against the Act. Do not let a request sit in the shared inbox during load-out week.
verdict_note: The third-party duty starts on 30 October. Before your first show after that, get harassment terms into the client contract and brief the crew, freelancers included. Name a person on site they can go to, and write down what you did.
